request: We've built a reporting add-on for our existing B2B product and want a go-to-market plan for selling it into a customer segment we've never targeted before.

objective.value: Win first customers for the reporting add-on in a segment the company has never sold to. No target number or outcome is stated yet (paying customers, pilots, revenue, or learning).
objective.evidence: Request: 'go-to-market plan for selling it into a customer segment we've never targeted before.' The intent to sell is stated; the outcome is not.

success_metric.evidence: Nothing stated. A leading indicator is needed (e.g. qualified demos, pilots started, activated accounts), with a counting rule that excludes existing-segment customers and free trials that never connect data.

icp.value: A 'new segment' is named but not identified: industry, company size, buyer role, and who it is NOT for are all unknown.
icp.evidence: Request: 'a customer segment we've never targeted before.' No further detail.

existing_distribution.value: The existing B2B customer base and its relationships are probably the only owned surface, and it probably does not match the new segment, so it is an upsell or referral route at best. Partners, lists, communities and brand awareness in the new segment are unknown.
existing_distribution.evidence: Deduced from 'existing B2B product' and 'never targeted before'. Unconfirmed; the segment-match question is the key unknown.

offer.value: A reporting add-on built for the existing B2B product. Whether new-segment buyers must adopt the core product first, or can buy it standalone, is unknown, and so are pricing, packaging and trial terms.
offer.evidence: Request: 'reporting add-on for our existing B2B product'. If it needs the core product, the offer is the whole product, not the add-on, which changes the plan.

objections.evidence: Not stated. Likely candidates are data handling and integration with systems already in place in the new segment, and switching cost. If the add-on handles financial or audit-relevant figures, trust and traceability become the decisive objection.

alternatives.evidence: Not stated. Impact is raised because the add-on will be priced, and the price anchor and positioning depend on what the new segment uses today (spreadsheets, BI tools, an incumbent).

channels.evidence: No channel named. Impact is raised above the default because the segment is new and no matching distribution is confirmed. Viable routes depend on the distribution answer, and any outbound route may carry unsolicited-contact rules.

unit_economics.value: Customer value and acceptable acquisition cost in the new segment are unknown.
unit_economics.evidence: Willingness to pay in a segment never sold to cannot be settled by conversation.
unit_economics.test_plan: Present 2-3 price points and packagings to 8-10 prospects from the segment in discovery calls, then run a paid pilot or letter-of-intent test. Compare the price accepted to the cost of reaching them.

capacity.evidence: Hours per week and number of weeks, and who is available (sales, marketing, product, founders), are not stated. This is the binding constraint on the plan.

budget.evidence: No budget stated, and nothing on whether it is committed or released on an early result.

horizon.evidence: No deadline or review date stated.

instrumentation.value: Assumed: the existing product's analytics and a CRM can count funnel stages. What cannot be measured (e.g. dark-social referrals) is not yet identified.
instrumentation.evidence: Deduced from the existing B2B product. Not confirmed, and low impact until channels are chosen.

decision_thresholds.evidence: No continue / change / stop criteria stated. They depend on the objective, metric and horizon.

questions.q: How many hours per week can your team actually give to this go-to-market, for how many weeks, and who are those people (sales, marketing, product, founders)?
questions.why: Uncertain × high: this is the binding constraint, and it decides how many channels and experiments the plan can hold.

questions.q: In the new segment, what do you already have: contacts, partners, a list, a community, or brand recognition? Or do your current customers include people who know or work with this segment?
questions.why: Uncertain × high: it is the main determinant of which channels are viable, and designing channels before knowing it is guesswork.

questions.q: Which segment is it (industry, company size, buyer role), and can you name a kind of company in it that you would NOT target?
questions.why: Uncertain × high: every message, channel and price depends on a narrow first slice.

questions.q: Can a company in the new segment buy the add-on without your core product? If not, what does a new customer have to adopt first, and on what terms (price, trial, contract)?
questions.why: Uncertain × high: an add-on that needs the core product means selling the whole product, which is a different plan and a longer sale.

questions.q: What would make a buyer in this segment hesitate or refuse? For example: data leaving their systems, integration with what they already use, audit or compliance requirements, or switching cost. What do you have to answer it (references, certifications, a pilot)?
questions.why: Uncertain × high: if the add-on handles sensitive or audit-relevant figures, this objection decides conversion.

questions.q: What does the segment use today for this reporting, and roughly what does it cost them (a tool, spreadsheets, an analyst, an agency)?
questions.why: Uncertain × high once priced: positioning and the price anchor are defined against what they already use.

questions.q: What outcome do you want, by when? For example: N paying customers or pilots, or a revenue figure, within a given number of months, or evidence that the segment is worth pursuing.
questions.why: Uncertain × high: it decides the plan's shape, and whether it should be a learning exercise or a scale-up.

questions.q: What budget is available, and is it committed or released only after an early result?
questions.why: Uncertain × medium-high: it decides whether paid acquisition or partnerships are possible, or whether the plan is limited to owned effort.

questions.q: Which early signal would you count as progress (e.g. demos booked, pilots started), and at what result would you continue, change course, or stop?
questions.why: Uncertain × high: without a leading indicator and a stop rule the plan cannot be judged before the horizon.

summary.objective: Build a go-to-market plan to sell a reporting add-on, built for the existing B2B product, into a customer segment the company has never targeted.
summary.scope: Segment definition, offer and packaging, positioning against current alternatives, a small set of channels fitted to available hours and existing distribution, and measurable thresholds for continuing or stopping. The target outcome and timeline still need to be set.
assumptions: The existing customer base is probably not in the new segment, so it is an upsell or referral route at best (inferred).
The add-on likely depends on the core product, which would make this a sale of the whole product (inferred, to confirm).
Standard analytics and a CRM can measure the funnel (inferred, low impact).
Willingness to pay in the new segment is untested and is treated as something to test, not assume.
summary.blind_spot: Two unknowns decide the plan: whether the add-on can be bought without the core product, and whether any distribution exists in the new segment. Without a matching audience and with a hard dependency on the core product, the add-on is not a quick upsell, and the plan has to be a pilot-led learning effort sized to the available hours.

objective.value: A go-to-market plan for a reporting add-on, aimed at a customer segment the company has never sold to. The outcome it must achieve (first customers, revenue, pipeline, or learning) is not stated.
objective.evidence: Request: 'want a go-to-market plan for selling it into a customer segment we've never targeted before.'

success_metric.evidence: No leading indicator or counting rule stated.

icp.value: Unknown new segment. Not stated who they are, what size they are, who buys, or who uses the product.
icp.evidence: Request only says 'a customer segment we've never targeted before'.

existing_distribution.value: The existing B2B customer base and its relationships probably exist, but they belong to the old segment. Nothing is known about reach into the new segment (list, partners, community, references).
existing_distribution.evidence: 'our existing B2B product' implies a current customer base. The segment is 'never targeted', so reach into it is probably thin. This is the assistant's deduction, not confirmed.

offer.value: A reporting add-on built on an existing B2B product. Unknown whether new-segment buyers must adopt the base product first (a two-step sale) or can buy the add-on standalone. Pricing, packaging and terms are unknown.
offer.evidence: Request: 'reporting add-on for our existing B2B product'. 'Add-on' implies a dependency on the base product, which is deduced and not confirmed.

objections.value: Unknown. Likely candidates are trust and data handling, switching cost, and whether the figures are auditable and tie back to the source. If the segment is finance or regulated, auditability becomes a hard requirement.
objections.evidence: Nothing stated. The candidates come from the financial-reporting and b2b-platform context cards, not from the requester.

alternatives.value: Unknown what the new segment uses today (spreadsheets, BI tools, an incumbent, an agency) or what it costs them. Impact is raised because the add-on will be priced, and price anchor and pitch are defined against that alternative.

channels.value: No candidate channels identified. Impact is raised because no existing distribution into the new segment is named, and a channel may carry a legal regime (unsolicited-contact rules) or a regulated audience.

unit_economics.evidence: No price, margin, sales-cycle or lifetime value given.

capacity.value: Unknown: people and hours per week available for go-to-market work, and for how many weeks.
capacity.evidence: Nothing stated. This is the binding constraint on how many channels the plan can include.

budget.evidence: No amount given, and unknown whether it is committed or conditional on an early result.

horizon.evidence: No date or review point given.

instrumentation.evidence: Nothing stated. The default is to use whatever CRM and product analytics already exist. Not worth a question yet.

decision_thresholds.evidence: No continue, change or stop criteria given. This follows once the objective, horizon and economics are known.

questions.q: How many people will work on this go-to-market, and how many hours per week each, for how many weeks (including sales, marketing and customer success time)?
questions.why: High uncertainty × high impact: the hours available set how many channels and experiments the plan can hold. A plan that doesn't fit the available time is not a plan.

questions.q: Which segment is this: industry, company size, and the role of the person who buys and the person who uses it? Can you name one type of company in that segment who is not a fit?
questions.why: High uncertainty × high impact: the segment sets the message, the channels and whether the buyer is regulated. Without it, nothing else in the plan can be sized.

questions.q: What do you already have in or near this new segment: existing customers who sit in it, partners or resellers, an email list, community presence, references or contacts? Or is it a cold start?
questions.why: High uncertainty × high impact: existing reach decides which channels are viable at all. It's better to know this before proposing anything new.

questions.q: Can someone in the new segment buy the add-on without already using your base product, or must they adopt the base product first? How is the add-on priced and packaged today?
questions.why: High uncertainty × high impact: a standalone sale and a base-product-plus-add-on sale are different sales motions, with different cycle lengths, pricing and onboarding.

questions.q: What is the one outcome this must achieve (for example a number of paying customers or a revenue target), and by when will it be judged?
questions.why: High uncertainty × high impact: the target and its deadline set the plan's ambition, its pace and the stop-or-continue decision. Horizon is covered here too.

questions.q: What does the new segment use today to get these reports (spreadsheets, BI tools, a competitor, an outsourced provider), and roughly what does it cost them?
questions.why: High uncertainty × high impact: positioning, the price anchor and the pitch are all defined against what the buyer already uses.

questions.q: What would make a buyer in this segment hesitate: sending their data into your product, the figures needing to be auditable, or the cost of switching? Does this segment have compliance requirements on its reporting?
questions.why: High uncertainty × high impact: if the segment is regulated or audit-sensitive, traceability becomes a build cost and an early gate in the sale.

questions.q: How much money is available for this go-to-market, and is it fully committed or released only if an early result comes in?
questions.why: Medium-high value: committed and conditional budgets lead to different plans (paid channels, events, a partner programme).

summary.objective: Define a go-to-market plan to sell an already-built reporting add-on into a customer segment the company has never targeted. The target outcome and the deadline are not yet stated.
summary.scope: Segment definition and buyer roles, positioning against what the segment uses today, offer and pricing, channels matched to existing reach, a plan sized to the hours and budget available, and a measurement and decision framework. The build is out of scope: the add-on is already built.
assumptions: The add-on needs the existing base product (inferred from the word 'add-on'), so a new-segment buyer may have to adopt both.
The existing customer base belongs to the old segment, so reach into the new one is probably weak.
Instrumentation defaults to the CRM and analytics already in place.
The reporting content may be audit-sensitive (financial-reporting context), which would raise the trust and traceability bar, but this is unconfirmed.
summary.blind_spot: Nobody has yet said how much time the team has, or what reach it has into the new segment. A plan built before those two are known risks a long channel list that nobody has the hours to run, aimed at an audience nobody can reach. A close second is whether the segment can buy the add-on without the base product.

objective.value: Win first paying customers for the reporting add-on in a new customer segment (not yet named). Target outcome and date not stated.
objective.evidence: Request: 'go-to-market plan for selling it into a customer segment we've never targeted before.'

success_metric.evidence: No leading indicator or counting rule given.

icp.value: Segment is unnamed; only known to be new to the company and B2B.
icp.evidence: Request: 'a customer segment we've never targeted before.'

existing_distribution.value: Existing B2B customer base and product exist, but the segment is new, so the existing audience likely does not match the ICP. Whether any list, partner or community reaches the new segment is unknown.
existing_distribution.evidence: Request: 'existing B2B product' and 'never targeted before'. Match to new segment is deduced, not stated.

offer.value: A reporting add-on to the existing product. Whether it is sold to new segment buyers who must also adopt the base product, or standalone, is unknown. Pricing and terms unknown.
offer.evidence: Request: 'reporting add-on for our existing B2B product'. Add-on dependency on the base product is a deduction. If the add-on needs the base product, the new segment may have to buy two things.

objections.value: Unknown. The add-on likely moves financial or operational data into the product, so trust, data handling and switching cost are probable blockers. If reporting touches financial figures, auditability and export requirements may decide conversion.
objections.evidence: Not stated. Inferred risk from the nature of reporting add-ons (see financial-reporting context).

alternatives.value: Unknown what the new segment uses today (spreadsheets, BI tools, accountants, a competitor). Impact raised because the add-on will be priced and positioned against that.

channels.value: No channels named. Impact raised because the segment is new and no existing distribution is confirmed to reach it. A channel with a legal regime (cold outreach) or a regulated segment would raise it further.

unit_economics.evidence: No price, margin, retention or CAC given.

capacity.value: Unknown how many people and hours per week are available for go-to-market work, and for how many weeks.
capacity.evidence: Not stated. This is the binding constraint on how many channels the plan can include.

horizon.evidence: No date or review point given.

instrumentation.value: Assume the existing product's analytics and CRM can count leads and conversions. Not confirmed.

questions.q: Which customer segment is this (industry, company size, the buyer's role), and who is it explicitly not for?
questions.why: High uncertainty and high impact: every other choice (offer, objections, channels, alternatives) depends on who the segment is, and a regulated segment would change the channel rules.

questions.q: How many people will work on this go-to-market, and how many hours per week each, for how many weeks?
questions.why: High impact: the plan has to fit the hours that exist, and this decides how many channels it can include.

questions.q: What already reaches this new segment today: an email list, a partner, a community, a few existing customers in the segment, or nothing?
questions.why: High impact: this largely decides which channels are viable. Starting from nothing leads to a different plan than starting from a partner or a warm list.

questions.q: Can the add-on be bought on its own, or only by customers who also use your base product? On what pricing and terms?
questions.why: High impact: if new-segment buyers must adopt the whole product, the sale and the objections are very different from a standalone add-on.

questions.q: What is the one outcome you want from this and by when (for example, N paying customers or a revenue figure within X months), and what early signal would you count as progress?
questions.why: High impact: without a target and a clock, nothing can be judged as working or not.

questions.q: What does this segment use today for reporting, and what does it cost them?
questions.why: The add-on's price and pitch are defined against what the buyer already uses, so this sets positioning.

questions.q: What would make a buyer in this segment hesitate: sending their data into your product, switching from what they have, or compliance and audit requirements?
questions.why: High impact: for a reporting add-on that handles the customer's data, this objection often decides whether they buy.

summary.objective: Build a go-to-market plan to sell the reporting add-on into a customer segment the company has never targeted. The target, the date and the success measure are not yet defined.
summary.scope: Likely scope: define the segment and its buyer, position the add-on against what the segment uses today, pick channels that fit the hours available, and set decision thresholds. Not yet scoped: the pricing, the product changes, and any compliance work.
assumptions: The add-on is sold as an extension of the existing B2B product, so new buyers may need the base product too.
The existing customer base and audience probably do not match the new segment.
The existing analytics and CRM can count leads and conversions.
summary.blind_spot: Nothing is known about the segment, the available hours, or whether any existing distribution reaches it. The plan cannot choose channels until these are answered, and if the add-on needs the base product, the sale is a bigger one than the request suggests.
